report:
Qualified **yes**: for women with **recurrent uncomplicated cystitis/UTI**, regular cranberry juice or extract can **reduce the risk of recurrence**, but it is not a guarantee and should not be used to treat an active infection.

The best synthesis is the 2023 Cochrane review: cranberry products probably lower symptomatic, culture-confirmed UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs, while evidence is weaker/negative in older institutionalized people, catheter users, and those with bladder-emptying problems; product dose and proanthocyanidin (PAC) content vary widely. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10636779/

Guidelines now reflect this: the AUA recurrent-UTI guideline says clinicians should offer cranberry as a prophylaxis option for women with recurrent UTIs (moderate recommendation, grade B), alongside other non-antibiotic and antibiotic strategies. https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/recurrent-uti

An early randomized trial found daily cranberry-lingonberry concentrate reduced recurrence over 12 months versus control, supporting biological plausibility via PACs blocking bacterial adhesion. https://www.bmj.com/content/322/7302/1571

Practical takeaway: choose a standardized product (often ~36 mg PAC/day) or consistent juice intake, expect a modest absolute benefit, watch sugar load with juice, and continue proven measures such as post-coital or continuous antibiotic prophylaxis when indicated, vaginal estrogen after menopause, and evaluation for red flags.
